title: Rohatsu 2010
speaker: Eko Jeff Kelley
summary: The main teaching of the talk is that our sense of self can be a source of suffering by adding unnecessary layers and expectations to our experience during meditation or sesshin. We often carry around an identity that we think will bring us affirmation and validation, but this can actually create more suffering when things don't meet our expectations. By letting go of this identity and simply observing our experiences without judgment, we can tap into a more authentic and bare essence of ourselves, allowing for greater clarity and understanding. This talk invites the listener to explore how their own sense of self is constructed and how it may be contributing to their suffering, with the goal of finding a more essential and peaceful way of being.

It's a great thing that we are here doing this sesshin, this two-and-a-half-day sesshin.

I can't remember; I think we were looking around last spring for a place on Kameno Island.
I can't remember, but we have been planning this, and now we're finally here.
I think one of the reasons that we have been thinking about this so much is that I think we both really value this practice of sesshin, this chance to deeply settle.
There's nothing really quite like it, this container with all its intricacy, and yet it's something that we can just totally let go into.
I've never found anything else quite like it, and it's been very important for me in my practice.
And so I encourage it wherever possible.
But sesshin is difficult, right?
It can be difficult.
We sit long hours, and there's lots of fussy little things to try to get right.
So I would like to talk a little bit today about that difficulty.
I think one of the reasons these things are difficult is that we add a lot of our own stuff to our experience.
We have this idea about ourselves that we carry around with us, and often our experience during sesshin is kind of at odds with that idea.
We either build ourselves up or tear ourselves down, always kind of swaying back and forth or responding to our experience and our evaluation of it.
So this morning at Oriochi, maybe some of you who were brand new were a little bit awkward and you kind of wondered, "Well, what does this mean about me?
I must be a real beginner here."
And maybe some of you who were very fluent in it started feeling like, "Wow, maybe I'm okay."
And some of us may have just the right clothes, while some of us don't feel like we really have a suitable outfit for this.
So we construct this identity out of our experience and continually patch it or smooth it or cleave it, depending upon the experience that arises.
And this creates suffering, right?
Because this is all in addition to the very essence of the experience—the sensation, the sound, the thought, the act.
These can all be engaged in without carrying this identity of ourselves around and without continually holding it up and looking to see how it's faring.
So this identity is probably an aspect of what we call the self, but I think it's one that we can see clearly in sesshin.

I think, not only because we have a chance to settle down and our mindfulness can be a little more precise and focused, but also because we have lots of chances to experience pain and mistakes and also occasional bliss.
So our patterns are very open, or our minds are very open, but our patterns are actually sometimes quite activated.
And so it's been my experience that the mind state during sesshin can take a lot of ups and downs.
So this is a good chance to see it, to see how it causes suffering and to see the possibilities for something a little different, something that's a little more bare and essential.
So I want to use the word identity here today, and one way that I'd like to look at it is that it's...
I think we're more attuned to the criticism that comes from ourselves, our self-critic or the self-praiser.
So we're kind of attuned to that feedback, and yet this identity that we have is really something that is shaped by that.
So this positive, what I'm calling identity, is sometimes not so clear.
We know we have it, and when we feel this criticism from within or without, we kind of modify it a little bit.
But what we actually carry around as our identity may not be all that visible.

But what allows us to coexist with our self-critical faculties is this idea that we have of ourselves and the idea that is the part of ourselves that is acceptable or even praiseworthy to this self-critic.
So it's kind of an amorphous thing, but I think we all know that we are carrying it.
So we're going to investigate that a little bit today.
I think most of us have grown up in this life very attuned and very seeking after affirmation.
So again, this is something that will help support, prop up this identity we have and avoiding things that might call it into question.
And of course, that right there is a recipe for suffering because all of the parts of ourselves that don't kind of fit, we want to split off and ignore and pretend they don't exist.
So it's a constant battle.
So our identity in another sense is the part of ourselves that suits our strategy for gaining affirmation from ourselves or from others.
This is the idea of ourselves that we use to gain affirmation, seek affirmation, and the rest of it we kind of split off.

And of course, this identity thrives on comparisons.
